Context. The previous page lists Riemann's six-fold transformation group of the P-function and an integral of Euler/Schwarz type. It also gives a connection formula of the form P(a,b,c,x) sin(b pi) = cos(...) P(-b,-a,c,1-x) - cos(...) P(b,-a,-c,1-x). The next page is lecture prose on the integrals I = int_0^1 y^alpha (1-y)^beta (1-xy)^delta dy. So P(a,b,c,x) here denotes a particular branch of Riemann's P-function with exponent differences a (at x=0), b (at x=1) and c (at x=infinity). It is normalised as an Euler integral. Pi(s) = Gamma(s+1) is Gauss's notation.

The exponents are taken symmetrically: 1/6 +- a/2 at 0, 1/6 +- b/2 at 1, 1/6 +- c/2 at infinity. Their sum is 1, as Riemann's 1857 convention requires. This is my inference from the factor 1/6 that appears on line 4.

Line 1 (change of normalisation c -> -c).
- P(a,b,c,x) is the branch at 0 with exponent 1/6 + a/2. Its leading coefficient is (my inference) the Euler-integral factor Gamma(beta') Gamma(gamma'-beta') / Gamma(gamma'), with gamma' = 1+a and beta' = (1+a+b+c)/2, so gamma'-beta' = (1+a-b-c)/2.
- In Riemann's notation this numerator is Pi((a+b+c-1)/2) Pi((a-b-c-1)/2).
- It is invariant under (b,c) -> (-b,-c), which matches line 4's P(a,b,c,x) = P(a,-b,-c,x).
- Replacing c by -c gives the same function of x (the hypergeometric series is symmetric in its two upper parameters). Only the factor changes, to Pi((a+b-c-1)/2) Pi((a-b+c-1)/2).
- Hence P(a,b,c,x) = [Pi(A) Pi(B) / (Pi(C) Pi(D))] P(a,b,-c,x), with A=(a+b+c-1)/2, B=(a-b-c-1)/2, C=(a+b-c-1)/2, D=(a-b+c-1)/2.

Line 2 (filled in by me).
- The reflection formula Pi(s) Pi(-s-1) = Gamma(s+1) Gamma(-s) = -pi/sin(pi s) gives 1/(Pi(C) Pi(D)) = Pi(-C-1) Pi(-D-1) sin(pi C) sin(pi D) / pi^2.
- So the ratio equals K sin(pi C) sin(pi D), where K = Pi(A) Pi(B) Pi(-C-1) Pi(-D-1) / pi^2.
- This isolates the trigonometric dependence of the connection coefficient.

Line 3.
- sin(pi(u-1)/2) = -cos(pi u/2). The two minus signs cancel, giving K cos(pi(a+b-c)/2) cos(pi(a-b+c)/2) P(a,b,-c,x).

Line 4.
- P(a,b,c,x) = P(a,-b,-c,x), the normalisation symmetry above.
- It also equals e^{+-(a/2+1/6) pi i} P(a,c,b,x/(x-1)). The Mobius map y = x/(x-1) fixes 0 and interchanges 1 and infinity, so the P-symbol with differences (a,b,c) becomes (a,c,b).
- The branch at 0, x^{1/6+a/2}(1+...), becomes (-y)^{1/6+a/2}(1+...). That produces the phase e^{+-(a/2+1/6) pi i}, with the sign set by the branch of log(-1).
- In Euler-integral form this is the substitution t -> 1-t, i.e. Pfaff's transformation F(alpha,beta;gamma;x) = (1-x)^{-alpha} F(alpha, gamma-beta; gamma; x/(x-1)). It swaps Gamma(beta') and Gamma(gamma'-beta'), so the normalisation is unchanged up to the phase.
- The line breaks off at 'P(a -'.

Line 5 (unfinished).
- The same scheme with a replaced by -a: P(-a,+-b,c,x) = P(-a,-+b,-c,x) = e^{...} P(-a, ...).

Purpose. The page is building a table of how the normalised branches transform under the sign changes of exponent differences and the substitutions x -> x/(x-1) etc. It is preparation for the connection formula between branches at 0 and 1 on the previous page and its lecture treatment on the next page.
